inline.s: {Among my disciples, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers. He knows the exact number of all the stars and all the living beings throughout the three thousand great thousand worlds in a single day and night. Suppose that living beings in the ten directions all became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of a trillion years and spiritual powers equal to Maudgalyāyana's. Exhausting their lifespans and straining their wisdom, they all together calculate the measure of Amitābha Buddha's lifespan — yet of a hundred parts they do not know one, and of a thousand parts, a hundred thousand parts, or even an u-pa-ni-sha-t'an-fen part,
they likewise do not know one.

Among my disciples, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers. Of all the stars and all the living beings in the three thousand great thousand worlds, he knows the full count once he has reckoned a single day and night. Suppose that all the living beings of the worlds in the ten directions became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of a trillion years and spiritual powers equal to Maudgalyāyana's. If they exhausted their lifespans and strained their wisdom to jointly calculate the measure of Amitābha Buddha's lifespan and the lifespans and numbers of the people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, of a hundred parts they could not know one part; of a thousand parts, a hundred thousand parts, or even an u-pa-ni-sha-t'an-fen part, they likewise could not know one part.
{U-pa-ni-sha-t'an-fen—This is the name for an analysis carried to the utmost subtlety. The Sound and Meaning of the Huìyuàn says:

“Suppose one splits a single hair into a hundred parts; then splits each of those parts into a hundred thousand parts; then splits those parts further still, until one reaches the neighboring-void, the point beyond which nothing can be split. That is what is called an u-pa-ni-sha-t'an-fen.”
The Sutra of the Assembly of Immeasurable Thus-Come Ones (Tang translation) says:

“Ānanda, the śrāvaka host of that Immeasurable Life Thus-Come One cannot be measured or known to its limit. Suppose there were monks numbering a full hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, every one of them like Mahāmaudgalyāyana, sovereign in spiritual powers, who in the morning hour traveled throughout a great thousand worlds and in an instant returned to where they were. Though they passed a hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of years, wishing together to reckon the śrāvakas of the first assembly of Immeasurable Life Buddha, exhausting their spiritual powers even to the end of their lives, of a hundred parts they would not know one; of a thousand parts, a hundred thousand parts, or even an u-pa-ni-sha-t'an-fen part, they likewise would not know one.”

{Suppose there is a great ocean, deep and vast beyond bounds. Take a single hair and split it into a hundred parts. With one of those parts, dip up a single drop of water from the great ocean. Which is more—this one drop of water, or the ocean? Ānanda, the number known by those Maudgalyāyanas is like this drop of water; what they do not know is like the water of the great ocean. The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha, and the lifespans and numbers of the people of that land, are likewise so: they are not to be known by reckoning or by metaphor.

Suppose there is a great ocean, deep and vast beyond bounds. Suppose one takes a single hair and splits it into a hundred parts, then with one of those parts dips up a single drop of water from the great ocean.

How does this one drop compare with all the water of the great ocean? Ānanda, the number reckoned by those pratyekabuddhas who are like Maudgalyāyana throughout a trillion years is like this one drop, while the number not yet reckoned is like all the water of the great ocean. The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha, and the lifespans and numbers of the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, are likewise so: they are not to be known by reckoning or by metaphor.

The foregoing explains that Amitābha Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable, that the lifespans of the beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are immeasurable, and that their numbers are immeasurable as well.

blocks.text: 14. Flowers and Trees Fill the Land

inline.s: {Again, Ānanda, that Land of Ultimate Bliss is replete with immeasurable merit and adorned in every way. Wondrous flowers of every kind fill it and spread their fragrance everywhere.

There are seven-jeweled banners arrayed in ordered rows throughout. Upon those jeweled banners hang canopies of every kind and bells of many jewels, complete in a hundred thousand subtle and varied hues.

Again, Ānanda, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is replete with immeasurable merit and adorned in every way. It is filled with wondrous flowers of every kind, and fragrance spreads in all four directions. There are seven-jeweled banners, arrayed in orderly rows and spread throughout. Upon those jeweled banners hang canopies of every kind and bells of many jewels, complete in a hundred thousand subtle and varied hues.
{Fragrance everywhere—The fragrance of grasses and flowers. {Varied hues—Many kinds of color.

{Ānanda, in that land of the Thus-Come One there are many jeweled trees: trees of pure gold, trees of pure silver, trees of pure lapis lazuli, trees of pure coral, trees of pure amber, trees of pure mother-of-pearl, trees of pure carnelian—each made of a single jewel alone, unmixed with any other. There are also trees formed jointly of two jewels, three jewels, or up to seven jewels, combined in turn. Their roots, stems, branches, and trunks are made of one jewel, while their flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from another—a convergence of many kinds.

Ānanda, the Land of Ultimate Bliss has a great many jeweled trees: trees of pure gold, trees of pure silver, trees of pure lapis lazuli, trees of pure coral, trees of pure amber, trees of pure mother-of-pearl, trees of pure carnelian—each made of a single jewel alone, unmixed with any other. There are also trees formed jointly of two jewels, three jewels, or up to seven jewels, combined in turn. The roots, stems, branches, and trunks of these trees are made of one jewel, while their flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from another, taking shape together.

{Each grows in its own row; row faces row, stem gazes upon stem, branches and leaves turn toward one another, flowers and fruits match one another; their glorious colors shine so brightly that the eye cannot take them all in. Nets of seven jewels spread over them, soft as tūla cotton. When a clear breeze rises from time to time, it sends forth the five tones, and the subtle notes of the scale naturally harmonize. These jeweled trees fill that land, their radiance so resplendent that nothing in the world can compare.

All these jeweled trees grow in rows according to their kind, neatly arrayed: stem gazes upon stem, branches and leaves turn toward one another, and fresh flowers and ripe fruits each hold the finest place, in brilliant colors and shining light, so bright and lovely that they are a joy beyond all telling. Nets of seven jewels spread over the trees, soft as tūla cotton. When a clear breeze blows from time to time, it sends forth most wondrous music, and the notes and melodies naturally answer one another. Jeweled trees such as these fill the entire Land of Ultimate Bliss, their radiance so dazzling that nothing in the world can compare.
{Five tones—The five notes of the Chinese pentatonic scale: gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu. {Subtle gong and shang—Here “gong and shang” stand for the five notes gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu.
They are used here to describe
wondrous music.
{Tūla cotton—The cotton produced by the tūla tree, like willow catkins.

{Moreover, at that site of enlightenment there is a bodhi tree, four million li in height. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas around, and its branches and leaves spread out on every side for two hundred thousand li. It is formed naturally of all kinds of precious substances. Its flowers and fruits bloom in splendor, and its radiance shines everywhere. There are also maṇi jewels of red, green, blue, and white — kings among jewels — that form its strings of jewels. Locks of cloud-gathering jewel adorn its jeweled columns. Golden bells and chimes
(duó)
Hang all around among its branches.

Moreover, at the site of enlightenment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a bodhi tree, four million li in height. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas around, and its branches and leaves spread out for two hundred thousand li. This tree is formed naturally of all kinds of precious substances. Its fresh flowers and ripe fruits are luxuriant and bright, and its radiance shines everywhere. There are also many wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels of red, green, blue, and white—kings among jewels—that form its strings of jewels. Interlocking ornaments made of cloud-gathering jewel adorn all its jeweled columns. Golden bells and wind-chimes hang throughout the branches of the bodhi tree.

{Site of enlightenment—The place where one studies and cultivates the Way. {Maṇi jewel—The wish-fulfilling jewel. {Strings of jewels—Ornaments strung from pearls and jade. {Locks of cloud-gathering jewel—Interlocking ornaments made of cloud-gathering jewel. “Cloud-gathering” is the name of a jewel. The Sutra of the Assembly of Immeasurable Thus-Come Ones (Tang translation) says:
“There are lion, cloud-gathering, and other such jewels, which form its locks and adorn its jeweled columns.”
“Suǒ (lock)” here means the interlocking structure within a building. {Bells and chimes (
duó
)—Wind-bells hung upon buildings.

{Precious and wondrous jeweled nets spread over it. A hundred thousand colors adorn one another, and immeasurable light blazes without limit; every adornment appears in response. A gentle breeze moves slowly, blowing through the branches and leaves and performing immeasurable wondrous Dharma-sounds. Those sounds flow abroad throughout all Buddha-lands. Clear and flowing, plaintive and bright, subtle and harmonious, they are foremost among all sounds in the worlds of the ten directions.

Precious and wondrous jeweled nets spread over the bodhi tree. In every jewel a hundred thousand colors adorn one another, and immeasurable light blazes without limit. Every adornment appears in response. A gentle breeze moves slowly, blowing through the branches and leaves and performing immeasurable wondrous Dharma-sounds. Those sounds flow abroad throughout the Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west. Clear and flowing, plaintive and bright, subtle and harmonious, they are foremost among all sounds in the worlds of the ten directions.
{In every jewel a hundred thousand colors—The Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:
“Each jewel has a thousand rays of light. Each ray of light has eighty-four thousand colors.”
{Without limit—Without bound. {Throughout all Buddha-lands—Throughout the Buddha-lands. Here “all” is a contraction of “of it.” For example: “cast them to the tail of the Bohai Sea.” (Liezi,
Questions of Tang) {Plaintive and bright—Winding and luminous.

{If there are living beings who behold the bodhi tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect the tree's merits, they all attain purity of the six senses and are free of every affliction; they abide in non-retrogression until they attain the Buddha Way. Moreover, by seeing that tree they obtain three kinds of tolerance: first, the tolerance of sound; second, the tolerance of compliance; third, the tolerance of the unborn Dharma.

If there are living beings who see the bodhi tree (eye), hear its sound (ear), smell its fragrance (nose), taste the flavor of its fruit (tongue), touch its light and shadow (body), or recollect the merits of the bodhi tree (mind), they all attain purity of the six senses, clear and transparent, and are free of every affliction; they abide peacefully in the stage of non-retrogression until they attain Buddhahood. Moreover, by seeing the bodhi tree they obtain three kinds of tolerance: first, the tolerance of sound; second, the tolerance of compliance; third, the tolerance of the unborn Dharma.

{Six senses—Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. {Tolerance—When the wisdom-mind abides peacefully in the true Dharma and is not dragged about by conditions, this is called tolerance. {Tolerance of sound—Awakening through sound to the truth that all dharmas are neither existent nor nonexistent, and thereby taming the mind so as to “not grasp at appearances but abide unmoving in suchness.” {All dharmas are neither existent nor nonexistent—All dharmas are illusory appearances, like things in a dream; they are not truly existent. (See
The True Nature of All Dharmas

.) {Tolerance of compliance—Meeting conditions and circumstances, one need not tame the mind, yet one naturally “does not grasp at appearances but abides unmoving in suchness.” At that time the mind is gentle and compliant. {Tolerance of the unborn Dharma—Abbreviated as the tolerance of the unborn: penetrating that all dharmas are originally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are empty just as they are; thus one abides peacefully in the unborn Dharma without the mind stirring. {No nature—Nature means substance; since all dharmas have no substantial reality (and are therefore illusory), this is called having no nature. The Lotus Sutra says:
“One knows that all dharmas are forever without nature.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“All illusions are without nature.”

{The Buddha told Ānanda: In such a Buddha-land, flowers, fruits, and trees all carry on the Buddha's work for the sake of living beings. This is all by the power of Amitābha Buddha's majestic spiritual might, by the power of his original vows, by the power of his fulfilled vows, and by the power of his clear, firm, and ultimate vows.

The Buddha told Ānanda: The Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus supreme, and its flowers, fruits, and trees all teach and transform every living being. This is all by the power of Amitābha Buddha's majestic spiritual might, by the power of his original vows, by the power of his fulfilled vows, and by the power of his clear, firm, and ultimate vows.

{Fulfilled vows—Vows that have been perfectly accomplished. {Clear, firm, and ultimate vows—The clear vow, the firm vow, and the ultimate vow. The Buddha Speaks of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Ānanda! If the gods and humans of that land, seeing this tree, obtain three Dharma-tolerances—first, the tolerance of sound; second, the tolerance of compliance; third, the tolerance of the unborn Dharma—this is all
(that is, all of it is)

by the power of the majestic spiritual might of Immeasurable Life Buddha, by the power of his original vows, by the power of his fulfilled vows, by the power of his clear vows, by the power of his firm vows, and by the power of his ultimate vows.”
{The clear vow—
The vow of true clarity.
{Moreover, the lecture halls and vihāras, the towers, terraces,
(guàn)

railings, and balustrades are all likewise formed naturally of seven jewels, and are further interwoven with white pearls and maṇi jewels, bright and wondrous beyond compare. The palaces in which the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.

Moreover, the lecture halls and vihāras, the towers, terraces, railings, and balustrades are all formed naturally of seven jewels, interwoven with white pearls and maṇi jewels, bright and wondrous beyond compare. The palaces in which the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.
{Vihāra—Another name for a temple. {Towers and terraces (
guàn
)—A general term for tall buildings such as towers and halls. {Railings and balustrades—Railings. “Lan” are the horizontal railings; “shun (
shǔn/dùn
)” are the vertical balusters. {Interwoven—Interlaced.

{Within it there are those on the ground expounding sutras and those reciting sutras; those on the ground receiving sutras and those listening to sutras; those on the ground walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation; and those in the open sky expounding and reciting, receiving and listening, walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation.

There, there are those on the ground expounding sutras, those reciting sutras, those on the ground receiving sutras, those listening to sutras, those on the ground walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation; and there are those in the open sky expounding sutras, reciting sutras, receiving sutras, listening to sutras, walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation.

{Some attain stream-entry, some attain once-returning, some attain non-returning, or arhatship. Those who have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression attain the stage of non-retrogression. Each recollects the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, and all are filled with joy.

They attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruits of non-returning and arhatship. Those who have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression attain the stage of non-retrogression. Each recollects the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, and all are filled with joy.

{The four fruits—The four fruit-stages of the śrāvaka vehicle, in order: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. {Non-retrogression—That is,
avaivartika
, which means: no falling back. This is to say that one reaches this stage only to advance step by step until attaining Buddhahood, never falling back in between.

{The Buddha told Ānanda: The Land of Ultimate Bliss has no seas, but has many rivers flowing and mingling everywhere, with golden sand spread over their beds. They are ten yojanas wide, or twenty, or thirty, or even a hundred thousand yojanas wide, and twelve yojanas deep.

The Buddha told Ānanda: The Land of Ultimate Bliss has no oceans, but has many rivers flowing and mingling everywhere. They are ten yojanas wide, or twenty, or thirty, or even a hundred thousand yojanas wide, and twelve yojanas deep.
{But has many rivers—The Sutra of the Assembly of Immeasurable Thus-Come Ones (Tang translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: That Land of Ultimate Bliss has no seas, but has many rivers. The narrowest of the rivers is a full ten yojanas across; the shallowest water is twelve yojanas deep. The depth and breadth of these rivers is twenty or thirty yojanas, or even a hundred. Some are exceedingly deep, and the broadest reaches a thousand yojanas. Their water is clear and cool and possesses the eight merits. Deep
(jùn)
currents surge without cease, sending forth subtle sounds.”
The Sutra of the Adornment of Immeasurable Life, Spoken by the Buddha (Song translation) says:

“In that Buddha-land, though there is no great ocean, there are springs and rivers flowing and mingling everywhere. Their water is ten yojanas broad, or twenty, or thirty, or even a hundred thousand yojanas, and twelve yojanas deep. Its water is pure and possesses the eight merits, sending forth subtle sounds, like the sounds of a hundred thousand kinds of music, throughout all Buddha-lands.”
Its water
is limpid, fragrant, and pure, its taste like sweet dew,
possessing the eight merits:

first, clear and pure; second, cool; third, sweet and lovely; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes immeasurable afflictions such as hunger and thirst; eighth, once drunk, it certainly nourishes the faculties and the four elements and increases all kinds of supreme roots of virtue.
Its water is clear, fragrant, and pure, its taste like sweet dew, and it possesses eight kinds of merit:

first, clear and pure; second, cool; third, sweet and lovely; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes immeasurable afflictions such as hunger and thirst; eighth, once drunk, it certainly nourishes body and mind and increases all kinds of supreme roots of virtue.
{Limpid—Clear and pure in appearance.

{The faculties and the four elements—Body and mind. “The faculties” are the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. “The four elements” are earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, and wind has motion. All tangible matter in the world (including the body) has these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion, and is therefore called an “element.” Here “the four elements” means the body.

{There are all kinds of famous flowers that float downstream. A gentle breeze stirs and sends forth all kinds of fragrance. On the two banks are fragrant candana trees, mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, with long boughs and dense leaves intercovering the river, blooming and bearing fruit, their fragrance and radiance a delight to behold. Multitudes of beings sport and roam at will. Some wade into the river and bathe
(zhuó, to wash)
and play in the current. Depth, shallowness, cold, and warmth all follow each person's liking. There are heavenly fragrances that scatter their scent
(fù, fragrance)
on the wind.

There are all kinds of famous flowers that float downstream. A gentle breeze stirs and sends forth all kinds of fragrance. On the two banks are many fragrant candana trees, mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, with long boughs and dense leaves intercovering the river, blooming and bearing fruit, fragrant and radiant, a delight to behold. Multitudes of beings sport and roam at will. Some wade into the river and bathe and play in the current. Depth, shallowness, cold, and warmth all follow people's liking. There are all kinds of heavenly fragrances that scatter their scent on the wind.

{The lecture halls and vihāras, and the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, have bathing pools inside and out, to left and right, ten yojanas across, or twenty or thirty, or even a hundred thousand yojanas, each equal in length and breadth. In a pool of gold, the bottom is sand of white silver; in a pool of white silver, the bottom is sand of gold; in a pool of crystal, the bottom is sand of lapis lazuli; in a pool of lapis lazuli, the bottom is sand of crystal; in a pool of coral, the bottom is sand of amber; in a pool of amber, the bottom is sand of coral; in a pool of mother-of-pearl, the bottom is sand of carnelian; in a pool of carnelian, the bottom is sand of mother-of-pearl; in a pool of white jade, the bottom is sand of purple gold; in a pool of purple gold, the bottom is sand of white jade. On the banks are fragrant candana trees, whose flowers and leaves hang down and spread, their fragrance pervading all.

Water of the eight merits fills them. When they wish to bathe, each enters a pool and bathes. Whether one wishes the water to reach the feet, the knees, the waist, the armpits, or the neck; whether one wishes it to pour over the body; whether one wishes it cold or warm, swift-flowing or slow—the water in each pool follows every wish, refreshing the spirit and delighting the body.

The lecture halls and vihāras, and the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, have bathing pools inside and out, to left and right, ten yojanas across, or twenty or thirty, or even a hundred thousand yojanas, each equal in length and breadth. In a pool of gold, the bottom is spread with sand of white silver; in a pool of white silver, the bottom is spread with sand of gold; in a pool of crystal, the bottom is spread with sand of lapis lazuli; in a pool of lapis lazuli, the bottom is spread with sand of crystal; in a pool of coral, the bottom is spread with sand of amber; in a pool of amber, the bottom is spread with sand of coral; in a pool of mother-of-pearl, the bottom is spread with sand of carnelian; in a pool of carnelian, the bottom is spread with sand of mother-of-pearl; in a pool of white jade, the bottom is spread with sand of purple gold; in a pool of purple gold, the bottom is spread with sand of white jade. On the banks are fragrant candana trees, whose flowers and leaves hang down and spread, their fragrance pervading all. Water of the eight merits fills them. When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each enters a pool and bathes. Whether they wish the water to reach the feet, the knees, the waist, the armpits, or the neck; whether they wish the water to pour over the body of itself; whether they wish it cold or warm, swift-flowing or slow—the water in each pool follows every one of their wishes, making the bather clear in spirit and joyful and at ease.

{The jeweled pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. It is formed in turn of the seven precious substances naturally. The sand at its bottom is all white pearls, moonbright pearls, and maṇi pearls. The water of the eight merits is pure as if formless;

jewels and sand reflect each other clearly, and no depth is left unillumined. Gentle ripples slowly swirl and pour into one another. On the banks are fragrant candana trees, auspicious-fruit trees, mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, whose fresh flowers and ripe fruits, radiant and ever fragrant, shine with light, exceedingly beautiful. Long boughs and dense leaves intercover the water. They send forth all kinds of fragrance, which nothing in the world can match, and along the current they diffuse their scent.

The seven-jeweled pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. It is formed in turn of the seven precious substances naturally. The sand at the bottom of its water is all white pearls, moonbright pearls, and maṇi pearls. The water of the eight merits is clear and formless, and the seven jewels and the pearl-sand reflect one another, so that no depth is left unillumined. Gentle ripples (tiny wavelets) slowly swirl and pour into one another.

On the banks are fragrant candana trees, auspicious-fruit trees, mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, whose flowers and fruits are ever fragrant, shining with light. Slender branches and dense leaves intercover the pool. They send forth all kinds of wondrous fragrance, which no fragrance in the world can match, and along the current they diffuse their scent.

{The waves send up immeasurable subtle sounds. Some hear the sound of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the sound of the pāramitās; the sound of stilling and pacifying, of stillness and quiescence; the sound of the unborn and the undying; the sound of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. Some hear the sound of no nature, no doing, and no self; the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sound of the sweet-dew anointing and the conferring of the stage. Having heard all such sounds, their minds become pure, free of all discrimination, upright and impartial, and their roots of virtue ripen. According to what they hear, they accord with the Dharma. Those who wish to hear it hear it alone;
(zhé, then)
those who do not wish to hear it hear nothing at all. They never fall back from the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The waves of the water send up immeasurable subtle sounds. Some hear the sound of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha), the sound of the pāramitās, the sound of stilling and pacifying, of stillness and quiescence, the sound of the unborn and the undying, the sound of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; some hear the sound of no nature, no doing, and no self, the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, joy, and equanimity, the sound of the sweet-dew anointing and the conferring of the stage. Having heard all such sounds, their minds become pure, free of all discrimination, upright and impartial, and their roots of virtue ripen. According to the Dharma they hear, body and mind accord with it. Those who wish to hear it hear it alone; those who do not wish to hear it hear nothing at all (not the least sound). They never fall back from the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

{The ten powers—The ten powers possessed by the Tathāgata: first, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, that is, the power to know the reasonableness and unreasonableness of all things; second, the power of knowing the karmic retributions of the three times, that is, the power to know the causal retributions of all living beings throughout the three times; third, the power of knowing all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, that is, the power to know all kinds of meditative concentration and liberating samādhis; fourth, the power of knowing the superiority and inferiority of the faculties, that is, the power to know whether living beings' faculties are superior or inferior and whether the fruits they attain are great or small; fifth, the power of knowing all kinds of understanding, that is, the power to know universally the different circumstances of living beings; sixth, the power of knowing all kinds of realms, that is, the power to know universally the different circumstances of living beings; seventh, the power of knowing the path that leads to all destinations, that is, the power to know the causes and effects of the paths practiced by all living beings; eighth, the power of the unobstructed heavenly eye, that is, the power to see with the heavenly eye the birth and death of living beings and the causes of their good and evil karma without obstruction; ninth, the power of the undefiled knowledge of past lives, that is, the power to know living beings' past lives and to know the undefiled nirvāṇa; tenth, the power of knowing the eternal severance of habitual tendencies, that is, the power to know truly that every residual trace of delusion is forever cut off and never arises again.

{No doing—No creating by causes and conditions. {No self—The absence of the self of the person and the self of dharmas. The self of the person is the failure to understand that the five aggregates are a false union, and the deluded grasping at body and mind as a real self; the self of dharmas is the failure to understand that all dharmas arise dependently and are empty by nature, and the deluded grasping at all dharmas as having real substance and function. The Diamond Sutra says:
“One who penetrates the Dharma of no self is called by the Tathāgata a true bodhisattva.”

{Arising dependently and empty by nature—“Arising dependently” means that all things in the world arise from the convergence of many conditions; “empty by nature” means that all dharmas formed by the convergence of many conditions are empty in their nature, without any true substance of their own.

{In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans are lofty in wisdom and penetrating in spiritual powers, all of one single kind, without any difference of appearance. Their countenances are upright and their features subtle, surpassing the world and rare indeed; neither gods nor humans, they all receive bodies of natural purity and emptiness and substance without limit.
In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans are lofty in wisdom and penetrating in spiritual powers, all entirely of one single kind,
without any difference of good and bad. Their

countenances are upright and their features subtle, surpassing the world and rare indeed; they are neither beings of the god realm nor beings of the human realm, and all receive bodies of natural purity and emptiness and substance without limit.

{Surpassing the world and rare indeed—The beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all born transformationally from lotus flowers, endowed with bodies of true golden hue and the thirty-two marks, and so are said to be “surpassing the world and rare indeed.” {All—Entirely, wholly. {Living beings—In the ten Dharma-realms, apart from the Buddha, the remaining nine realms are all called living beings. {The ten Dharma-realms—Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four noble realms. The four noble realms are not subject to rebirth, while the six ordinary realms revolve through birth and death.

{The Buddha told Ānanda: Suppose a poor beggar of the world stood beside a king—could their features and appearance be reckoned alike? And if a king were compared with a wheel-turning sage king, he would be coarse and ugly, just as the beggar is beside the king. The wheel-turning sage king, foremost in majestic appearance, compared with the Heaven King Śakra, is again ugly and inferior. And if the Heaven King Śakra were compared with the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations, a hundred thousand times would not come near. If the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations were compared with the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the radiance of their countenances, a trillion times would not come near.

The Buddha told Ānanda: Suppose a poor beggar of the world stood beside a king—could their features and appearance be of one kind? And if a king were compared with a wheel-turning sage king, he would be coarse and ugly, just as the beggar is beside the king. The wheel-turning sage king, foremost in majestic appearance, compared with the Heaven King Śakra, is again ugly and inferior. If the Heaven King Śakra (Śakra) were compared with the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations (the sixth heaven king), the difference would be more than a hundred thousand times. If the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations were compared with the radiance of the countenances of the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the difference would be more than a trillion times

{The six heavens of the realm of desire—The realm of desire has six heavens: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; fifth, the Heaven of Delighting in Transformation; sixth, the Heaven of Enjoying Others' Transformations.

{The palaces in which they dwell, their clothing, food, and drink, are like those of the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations. As for their majesty, virtue, stage, and spiritual transformations, all gods and humans cannot be compared with them; a hundred thousand trillion times cannot measure the difference.

The palaces in which the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans of the Land of Ultimate Bliss dwell, and their clothing, food, and drink, are like those of the Heaven King of Enjoying Others' Transformations. As for their majesty, virtue, stage, and spiritual transformations, all beings of the god realms in other worlds cannot be compared with them; the difference is far more than a hundred thousand trillion times and cannot be measured.
{Ānanda, you should know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha, with such merit and adornment, is inconceivable!
Ānanda, you should know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha is thus adorned with merit, inconceivable!

{Again, all living beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—whether already born there, now being born there, or yet to be born there—all obtain such wondrous bodies. Their features are upright and majestic, their merit and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and their spiritual powers sovereign. All kinds of enjoyments are wholly abundant. Palaces, clothing and adornments, fragrant flowers and canopies, and every article of adornment come at will, exactly as they are thought of.

Again, all living beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—whether already born there (or already born here), now being born there (or now born here), or yet to be born there (or to be born here)—all obtain such wondrous bodies. Their features are upright and majestic, their merit and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and their spiritual powers sovereign. All kinds of enjoyments are wholly abundant. Palaces, clothing and adornments, fragrant flowers and canopies, and every article of adornment come at will, exactly as they are thought of.

{When they wish to eat, seven-jeweled bowls appear before them of themselves, and food and drink of a hundred flavors fills them of itself. Though such food is there, there is in truth no one who eats. They merely see its color and smell its fragrance and eat with the mind; their strength of form increases, yet there is no waste or impurity. Body and mind are soft and pliant, with no clinging to flavor. When the matter is done, it vanishes; when the time comes, it appears again.

When they wish to eat, seven-jeweled bowls appear before them of themselves, and food and drink of a hundred flavors fills them of itself. Though these fine dishes and delicacies are there, they are not swallowed into the belly. One need only see the color and smell the fragrance and eat with the mind; then the strength of form increases, and there is no waste or impurity. Body and mind are soft and pliant, with no greed or clinging. When the meal is done, the seven-jeweled bowls vanish of themselves; when they wish to eat again, the bowls are again filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors and appear of themselves.
{There are also wondrous garments made of many jewels, crowns, sashes, and strings of jewels, with immeasurable light and a hundred thousand wondrous colors, all complete and naturally upon the body.

There are also wondrous garments made of many jewels, crowns, sashes, and strings of jewels; they have immeasurable light and a hundred thousand wondrous colors, all complete and, according to each one's wish, naturally worn upon the body.

{The dwellings in which they live are of shapes and colors to their liking. Jeweled nets spread over them, and jeweled bells hang there. Wondrous, rare, and precious things adorn them everywhere. Light and color flash and shine, exceedingly majestic and fair. Towers, terraces, railings, and balustrades; halls, chambers, and pavilions—broad or narrow, square or round, large or small, some in the open sky, some on level ground. Pure, calm, and secure, subtly wondrous and joyful. They appear before them as their thoughts arise, and nothing is lacking.

For all living beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the dwellings in which they live—their shapes, sizes, colors, and arrangements—are wholly to their liking. Jeweled nets cover them, and all kinds of jeweled bells hang there. Wondrous, rare, and precious jewels adorn them everywhere. Light and color flash and shine, exceedingly majestic and fair. Towers, terraces, railings, and balustrades; halls, chambers, and pavilions—broad or narrow, square or round, large or small, some in the open sky, some on level ground. Pure, calm, and secure, subtly wondrous and joyful. They appear before them as their thoughts arise, and nothing is lacking.
{Adorn—To decorate.

blocks.text: 20. Winds of Virtue and Rains of Flowers

inline.s: {In that Buddha-land, at every mealtime, a natural wind of virtue rises gently and joyously and blows through the nets and all the jeweled trees. It sends forth subtle sounds, expounding suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no self, and all the pāramitās, and diffuses ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant fragrant virtue. Whoever hears it finds that dust and toil, defilement and habit, naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a monk who has attained the cessation concentration.

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, at every mealtime, a natural wind of virtue rises gently and joyously and blows through the nets and all the jeweled trees, sending forth subtle sounds that expound suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no self, and all the pāramitās, and diffuses ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant fragrant virtue. Whoever hears it finds that their afflictions (dust and toil) and bad habits (defilement and habit) naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a monk who has attained the cessation concentration.
{Wind of virtue—

The pure breeze that is replete with ten thousand virtues in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. {Suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no self—Suffering means that this brief human life has three kinds of suffering, eight kinds of suffering, and immeasurable sufferings; emptiness is arising dependently and being empty by nature—arising dependently means that all dharmas in the world arise from the convergence of many conditions, and being empty by nature means that all dharmas formed by the convergence of many conditions are empty in their nature, without any true substance of their own; impermanence is the impermanence of all formations, meaning that all dharmas in the world change without cease and arise and perish without end, with no permanent and unchanging entity; no self means that the person formed by the false union of the five aggregates has no truly unchanging self-substance to be found. {The five aggregates—Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—the five great elements that constitute a person. {The cessation concentration—Also called the concentration of the cessation of feeling and perception; this is the meditative concentration in which the six consciousnesses and their mental factors are extinguished and not allowed to arise. {Mental factors—Short for dharmas belonging to the mind, that is, the various psychological phenomena that belong to the mind.

{It also blows through the seven-jeweled groves and trees, and the drifting flowers gather in heaps, their many-colored lights filling the Buddha-land. They arrange themselves in order according to color, never in disorder. Soft, luminous, and pure, like tūla cotton. When one sets foot on them, they sink four finger-breadths; when the foot is lifted, they return to what they were. After mealtime has passed, the flowers disappear of themselves and the great earth is pure. According to the season, new flowers rain down again and again and spread throughout once more, no different from before—and so six times over.

The natural wind of virtue also blows through the seven-jeweled groves and trees; the drifting flowers gather in heaps (like flower beds), flashing with many-colored lights that fill the Buddha-land. They are arranged in order according to the colors of the flowers, never in disorder. These fresh flowers are soft, luminous, and pure, like tūla cotton; if one sets foot on them, they sink four finger-breadths, and when the foot is lifted, they return to what they were. After the meal has passed, these flowers disappear of themselves and the great earth is pure. According to the season (morning, midday, sunset, first watch, middle watch, and last watch), new flowers rain down again, and this is repeated throughout the Buddha-land. Six times each day, and so it is every time.
{Tread—To step on. {Four finger-breadths—That is, what is commonly called four horizontal fingers: the breadth of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers held together.

{Moreover, jeweled lotuses of many treasures fill the world all around. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand koṭis of petals. The light of these flowers is of immeasurable kinds and colors. Blue flowers emit blue light, white flowers emit white light; for black-red, yellow, vermilion, and purple, the light and color are likewise so. There are also immeasurable wondrous jewels and a hundred thousand maṇi pearls, reflecting and adorning rare treasures, outshining the sun and moon.

Moreover, jeweled lotuses of many treasures fill the entire Land of Ultimate Bliss. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand koṭis of petals. These jeweled lotuses radiate light in immeasurable and endless kinds of colors. Blue flowers emit blue light, white flowers emit white light, and the light and color of black-red (dark black with a touch of red), yellow, vermilion (bright red), and purple are likewise so (for example: yellow flowers emit yellow light). Upon the flowers there are also immeasurable wondrous jewels and a hundred thousand maṇi pearls, reflecting and adorning rare treasures, their radiance outshining the sun and moon.
{Black-red—Dark black with a touch of red.

{These lotuses measure half a yojana, or one, two, three, or four, or even a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower issue thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of rays of light. From each ray of light issue thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of Buddhas, of purple-gold bodily hue, with extraordinary marks and excellences. Each of these Buddhas again sends forth a hundred thousand rays of light, proclaiming the subtle Dharma everywhere for the ten directions. Thus each Buddha establishes immeasurable living beings in the true Buddha Way.

The diameter of those jeweled lotuses is half a yojana, or one, two, three, or four yojanas, or even a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower issue thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of rays of light. From each ray of light appear thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of Buddhas, of purple-gold bodily hue, with extraordinary marks and excellences. Each Buddha again sends forth a hundred thousand rays of light, proclaiming the subtle Dharma everywhere for the ten directions. Thus each Buddha establishes immeasurable living beings in the true Buddha Way.

{All who are reborn in the worlds of the ten directions are born transformationally of themselves in the lotuses of the seven-jeweled pools. They all receive bodies of purity and emptiness and substance without limit. They do not hear even the names of the evil afflictions and sufferings of the three evil paths. Since even the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering! There is only the sound of natural joy. Therefore that land is called Ultimate Bliss.

All who are reborn in the worlds of the ten directions are born transformationally of themselves in the lotuses of the seven-jeweled pools. They all receive bodies of purity and emptiness and substance without limit. They do not hear even the names of the evil afflictions and sufferings of the three evil paths. Since even the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering! They hear only the sounds of natural joy. Therefore that land is called Ultimate Bliss.
{Bodies of purity and emptiness and substance without limit—This is interlocking parallelism, meaning:
bodies of purity, emptiness, and limitlessness

. Since they are not nourished by food and drink, they are called pure and empty; since they are not destroyed by old age and death, they are called without limit. {Interlocking parallelism—Also called interlocking phrasing, a rhetorical device often used in ancient Chinese. Its characteristic is that it is not wordy, not redundant, and not flatly narrated, but implicit and concise, sparing in words while preserving the meaning, with the two parts completing each other's sense and enhancing each other's brilliance. For example, in “Song of Mulan,” “Generals and warriors died in a hundred battles; stalwart men returned after ten years” means: generals and warriors fought a hundred battles and died, and generals and warriors returned after ten years. Another example is “The Record of Yueyang Tower”: “Not delighted by things, not saddened by oneself” means: one is neither delighted by things nor by oneself, and neither saddened by things nor by oneself. Here “things” refers to people other than oneself and the circumstances in which one finds oneself, and “oneself” refers to one's personal fortunes.

blocks.text: 22. Abiding in the Assembly of Certainty

inline.s: {Again, Ānanda, in that Buddha-land there are no signs of gloom, of firelight, of sun, moon, and stars
(yào)

or of day and night, nor any names of years, months, or kalpas, nor any dwelling attached to household or family. In every place there are neither markers nor names, nor any discrimination of taking and rejecting; there is only the enjoyment of purity and the highest happiness.

Again, Ānanda, the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no sights of gloom, firelight, sun, moon, stars, day, or night, nor any names of years, months, or kalpas, and still less does it have dwelling in households and families as in the world. In every place there are neither names of streets and districts nor any discrimination of taking and rejecting, good and bad, beautiful and ugly; there is only the enjoyment of purity and the highest happiness.
{Yào (yào)—The sun, moon, and stars are all called “yào.” For example, the sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are together called the “seven luminaries.”
{Still less—
In the text there are three “no's” in succession (“
there are no
signs of gloom, firelight, sun, moon, and stars, or of day and night,
nor any
names of years, months, or kalpas,
nor any
dwelling attached to household or family”). Therefore “nor any” is rendered as “still less.”

{If there are good men and good women who are already born or yet to be born, they all abide in the assembly of certainty and are certain to realize anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is that? Because those in the assembly of wrong certainty and the assembly of uncertainty cannot understand and establish that cause.

If there are good men and good women, whether already reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss or yet to be reborn there, so long as they are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss they all abide in the assembly of certainty and are certain to attain Buddhahood (certain to realize anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi). Why is that? Because those who abide in the assembly of wrong certainty and the assembly of uncertainty cannot understand how to create (establish) the cause of Buddhahood.

{If there are good men and good women who are already born or yet to be born, they all abide in the assembly of certainty—An earlier passage (“11. The Vow to Abide in the Assembly of Certainty”) says:
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land do not abide in the assembly of certainty
(the assembly of right certainty)
and are not certain to reach cessation, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

blocks.text: 23. Praise by the Buddhas of the Ten Directions

inline.s: {Again, Ānanda, in the worlds of the east as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each world Buddhas as numerous as those sands each extend their broad and long tongues, emit immeasurable light, speak words of truth, and praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha. In the worlds of the south, west, and north as numerous as those sands, the Buddhas' praise is likewise so. In the worlds of the four intermediate directions and of above and below, as numerous as those sands, the Buddhas' praise is likewise so.

Again, Ānanda, in the worlds of the east as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each world the Buddhas, as numerous as those sands, each extend their broad and long tongues, emit immeasurable light, speak words of truth, and praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha. The Buddhas of the worlds of the south, west, and north as numerous as those sands praise in the same way. The Buddhas of the worlds of the four intermediate directions (southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast) and of above and below, as numerous as those sands, praise in the same way.

{Broad and long tongue—One of the Buddha's thirty-two marks. The Buddha's tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin, and can cover his face up to the hairline. Since his tongue has such a mark, his words are certainly true.

{Why is that? It is to cause all living beings in other directions to hear that Buddha's name, give rise to a pure mind, recollect and uphold it, take refuge, and make offerings. And if they can give rise to a single thought of pure faith, and with all their roots of virtue sincerely dedicate it, wishing to be born in that land, then they are all born there according to their wish and attain non-retrogression, and even the unsurpassed, right, and equal enlightenment.

Why do the Buddhas of the ten directions praise him thus? It is to cause all living beings in other worlds to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha, give rise to a pure mind, recollect and uphold it, take refuge, and make offerings. And if they can give rise to a single thought (unmixed with deluded thoughts) of pure faith, and sincerely dedicate all their roots of virtue, wishing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west, then they are all born there according to their wish and attain the stage of non-retrogression (no falling back again), and even Buddhahood.

{A single thought—A thought that is pure and single (unmixed with deluded thinking). Here “a single thought” does not mean an extremely brief instant (the span of a single thought) or one single act of thought.
The key to rebirth in the three grades: giving rise to the bodhi mind and single-minded, exclusive mindfulness.

{Giving rise to the bodhi mind—Giving rise to the great mind that seeks the Buddha Way above (perfect enlightenment, Buddhahood) and transforms living beings below. {Single-minded, exclusive mindfulness —
Always mindfulness of the Buddha with one mind, without any other thoughts
(see
Single-Minded, Exclusive Mindfulness
for a detailed account
Concerning single-minded, exclusive mindfulness, Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
Continue without interruption, and one is born
. If one can
continue thought after thought
to the end of one's life
, then ten people, ten are born; a hundred people, a hundred are born.
May all people ponder this well: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must
steel the mind and master oneself
never ceasing day or night
, so that as the former thought ends at death, the latter thought is born.
Forever enjoying the Dharma-bliss of non-doing, and even attaining Buddhahood—is this not a joy beyond measure!

{Continue without interruption, and one is born—At the moment of death, one need only keep the thought of the Buddha unbroken (not interrupted by deluded thoughts) and one is at once reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west. {If one can continue thought after thought to the end of one's life, then ten people, ten are born; a hundred people, a hundred are born—If one can continue the thought of the Buddha without interruption and practice thus for a lifetime (
that is, one of single-minded, exclusive mindfulness

), then of ten people, ten are born; of a hundred people, a hundred are born. {Steel the mind and master oneself—To steel the mind is to urge it on to do what should be done; to master oneself is to restrain oneself from doing what should not be done. These four words, “steel the mind and master oneself,” are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles. {Never ceasing day or night—Neither by day nor by night should one stop the unbroken succession of thoughts. {As the former thought ends at death, the latter thought is born—This means: because the thought of the Buddha continues unbroken, the final thought at the moment of death is certainly the thought of the Buddha, and immediately after that final thought one is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west.
(see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
The Buddha told Ānanda: The gods and people of the worlds of the ten directions who with sincere hearts wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.
The Buddha told Ānanda: Among the gods and people of the worlds of the ten directions, those who
with sincere hearts
(with the most sincere devotion) wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west fall into three grades (three ranks).
The Buddha Speaks of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
“The Buddha told Ānanda: The gods and people of the worlds of the ten directions who with sincere hearts wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.”
Those of the highest grade leave household life behind, renounce desire, and become monks.
They give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly, exclusively invoke Amitābha Buddha

, cultivate all merits, and vow to be born in that land. When such living beings approach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha with the great assembly appears before them, and they follow that Buddha and are born in his land. There, born transformationally of themselves in the lotuses of the seven-jeweled pools, they abide in non-retrogression, keen in wisdom and courageous, sovereign in spiritual powers. Therefore, Ānanda, if there are living beings who wish to see Amitābha Buddha in this present life, they should give rise to the unsurpassed bodhi mind, cultivate merit, and vow to be born in that land.

Those of the highest grade (the highest rank) who are reborn: they leave household life behind, renounce desire, shave their heads, and become monks; they give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly, exclusively invoke Amitābha Buddha, cultivate all merits, and vow to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west. When such living beings approach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha with the great assembly appears before them, and they follow Amitābha Buddha and are born in his land. There, born transformationally of themselves in the lotuses of the seven-jeweled pools, they abide in non-retrogression, keen in wisdom and courageous, sovereign in spiritual powers. Therefore, Ānanda, if there are living beings who wish to see Amitābha Buddha in this present life, they should give rise to the unsurpassed bodhi mind, cultivate merit, and vow to be born in that land.
{Those of the middle grade, though unable to leave home and become monks or to cultivate merit on a grand scale,
should give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly, exclusively invoke Amitābha Buddha

, and cultivate goodness to whatever extent they can. They observe the precepts and the fasts, erect stūpas and images, feed monks, hang silk banners and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense, and with this they dedicate the merit, vowing to be born in that land. At the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha manifests a transformed body, whose light and excellent marks are fully like the true Buddha, and with the great assembly appears before them. They follow the transformed Buddha and are born in that land, abide in non-retrogression, and in merit and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.
